title: The Educated Barbarian: Meditations analysis (part. 11)
summary: Part 11 of NH's Meditations reading, ending Book 5. He covers chaos as the engine of human evolution, focusing on the present, judging yourself by your impact rather than by fame, not engaging with people who wrong you, accepting your lapses without moralising, and helping instead of getting angry. He ends by disagreeing with Marcus on slavery and on never using harsh words.
claims: Instability and chaos are why humans evolved; creatures without challenges or predators have not changed for millions of years
Only the present can be seized; the past is mostly unknown and the future too vast to see, so worrying about it is a waste
Judge success by your positive impact on your community, not by fame; better to have an impact and be forgotten than be remembered with no impact
When suffering, focusing on yourself makes time slow down; what hurts is mostly how you receive the event, not the event itself
Being part of a bigger whole does not make you small; thinking nothing matters because it will vanish leads to a dangerous no-point-in-succeeding mindset
Whether someone's wrong hurts you is up to you; saying you do not care while reacting still means you care
Only engage with forces you intend to destroy or fix; otherwise move on without a single thought, since you are the only one keeping the event alive
Stoics will fail; when you lose control and act on a passion, accept it was your nature, because addicts never recover without first accepting they have a problem
After a lapse, assess it but do not pass moral judgment on yourself; self-flagellation feeds the cycle of repetition
Do not get angry at someone who unknowingly offends, like someone with body odour; help them kindly, and if they refuse, move on
Some things should transcend any era, such as knowing you should not own another person; Marcus urging kindness while listing his slaves is hypocritical
Harshness has a place; always taking the high road lets people learn there are no consequences, and the only way to stop them is consequences
There is no such thing as an unkind word in itself; it depends on who receives it and the intent, and French people speak harshly by culture
